opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a perfectly rational choice, and for most automakers it's probably the right one, at least for now.

You have to separate two things that people often lump together. One is autonomous driving as a *technology capability*, the perception, the planning, the decision-making stack. The other is robotaxi as a *business model*, which means owning or managing fleets, dispatching, remote operations, insurance, maintenance, dealing with city regulators street by street. These are very different businesses. A car company is fundamentally good at designing, manufacturing, and selling vehicles at scale. Running a mobility service is closer to operating an airline or a logistics company. Not every automaker wants that, and not every automaker should.

So what many of them are doing is taking the incremental path: L2, L2-plus, highway pilot, urban navigation assist, and moving gradually toward L3 and eventually L4 in certain conditions. That has real advantages. Every car sold becomes a data collector. You get millions of vehicles driving billions of kilometers, which is enormously valuable for training, especially for long-tail scenarios. And you earn revenue along the way instead of burning cash for ten years waiting for full driverless operation to work.

But I would add one caution. The step from "the human is responsible" to "the system is responsible" is not a linear extension. It's a phase change. Safety validation, redundancy in hardware, and the whole liability framework are qualitatively different at L4. Robotaxi companies, by operating truly driverless in limited areas, are forced to confront those hardest problems head-on. Automakers that only do assisted driving can sometimes postpone them, and there's a risk of underestimating how big that last gap is.

So my view is that the two routes are complementary, not competing. Ultimately I expect convergence. Robotaxi players need automakers to build purpose-designed vehicles at scale and at low cost, and automakers need the full-stack driverless know-how and operational experience. We'll see more partnerships, with some companies providing the "brain," others the "body," and others the operating platform. The industry is big enough that you don't have to do everything yourself. You just have to be very clear about which part you're best at.

r001.rationale: The response describes automakers and robotaxi operators as complementary and predicts partnerships and convergence. It does not clearly predict that the separation between manufacturing and taxi operation will persist.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes autonomous-driving technology from the robotaxi business model and mentions vehicle makers and operating platforms, but it does not divide the industry into services, vehicles, and chips and components.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a very rational choice, and honestly it reflects a split in the industry that has been there since the beginning. There are really two paths to autonomy. One is the robotaxi path, where you take out the driver entirely, run a fleet in a geofenced area, and operate it as a service. The other is the mass-production path, where you ship cars to consumers with progressively more capable driver assistance, and you use the fleet to collect data and improve the system over time.

Automakers naturally gravitate toward the second path because that is their business. They know how to design, manufacture, and sell cars at scale. They do not know how to run a transportation service, and they do not want to carry the capital cost of owning and operating a fleet, maintaining it, dealing with insurance, dealing with city-by-city regulation. Those are very different competencies, and the economics are very different too. A car company makes money when it sells a car. A robotaxi company makes money per mile, and it takes a long time and a lot of capital before that turns positive.

The real question is whether you can get to full autonomy through the consumer car route alone. My view is that the two paths are converging, but they converge from different directions. The robotaxi players have the safety and L4 engineering discipline but limited scale and high cost per vehicle. The automakers have enormous scale and data, but their systems are designed with a human in the loop, and the leap from "the driver is responsible" to "the car is responsible" is not just a software upgrade. It is a change in sensor suite, redundancy, validation, and liability.

So what I expect is partnership rather than one side winning. Automakers will supply the vehicle platform at consumer cost, and autonomy companies will supply the L4 stack and operating know-how. We already see this happening. An automaker that decides not to run robotaxis is not stepping away from autonomy. It is deciding which layer of the stack it wants to own. That is fine, as long as they do not mistake a good L2 or L3 product for a path that automatically leads to L4. It does not, at least not without deliberate investment in the hard parts.

r001.rationale: The response predicts partnership, with automakers supplying vehicles and autonomy companies providing the L4 stack and operating know-how, while automakers may choose not to run robotaxi services. This communicates a continuing division between vehicle manufacturing and taxi operation.

r002.rationale: The response discusses vehicle manufacturing and robotaxi services, but it does not divide the industry into three layers or identify chips and vehicle components as a layer.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a reasonable choice. Building an autonomous vehicle and operating a robotaxi service are two different businesses. An automaker has to develop the technology, integrate it into the vehicle, manufacture it reliably, and sell it. A robotaxi operator also has to manage a fleet, maintain and clean the vehicles, serve passengers, and achieve sufficient utilization to make the economics work.

An automaker doesn’t necessarily need to do all of that itself. It can provide vehicles and autonomous driving capabilities, then work with an operating partner. The important thing is to have a close feedback loop between vehicle development and real-world operation, so that each improves the other.

I wouldn’t judge the strategy simply by whether a company operates robotaxis. I would ask whether it has a clear role, whether its technology is safe and reliable, and whether the business model makes sense.

r001.rationale: The response describes manufacturing and robotaxi operation as separate businesses and says automakers can partner with operators, but it does not predict that this separation will persist in the autonomous-driving era.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes vehicle development from robotaxi services, but does not identify chips and components as a third industry layer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a reasonable choice. Building an autonomous car and operating a robotaxi service are two different businesses. An automaker’s strengths are in vehicle engineering, manufacturing, and sales. A robotaxi operator also has to manage fleets, dispatch vehicles, maintain them, and provide a reliable service every day.

The key is whether the automaker can still build a strong feedback loop between real-world driving data and improvements to the system. You don’t necessarily have to operate your own robotaxi fleet to do that; you can work with an operating partner. But you do need clear responsibility for safety and a sustainable business model. I don’t think every company needs to do everything.

r001.rationale: The response says manufacturing and robotaxi operation are different businesses and that companies need not do everything, but it does not predict that this separation will persist in the autonomous-driving era.
